Package and Data Load

The covid_deaths data frame includes data extracted from Oxford, it includes Time series data from Jan 1, 2020 to December 31 2023. Link to Data: https://ourworldindata.org/covid-deaths

Here is a link to the codebook explaining all the variables used: https://github.com/OxCGRT/covid-policy-dataset/blob/main/documentation_and_codebook.md

The covid_stringency is raw data extracted from the git-hub repository of Oxford. Link to Data: https://github.com/OxCGRT/covid-policy-tracker/tree/master/data

The income_categories data frame includes data extracted from the World Bank, they categorize world countries in High-income, Low-Income, Lower-Middle-Income and Higher-Middle-Income countries. Link to Data: https://datahelpdesk.worldbank.org/knowledgebase/articles/906519-world-bank-country-and-lending-groups

The world_map data frame is extract a data set pre-existing in R that has longitudes and latitudes for the world map.

Filtering and Cleaning the Data

#The location variable includes world and continent level variables that was skewing the graph, creating this to filter out these observations. This is only true for Covid_deaths, Covid_stringency is raw data. 
covid_combined_data <- 
  c("World", "Asia", "Europe", "Africa", "North America", "South America", "European Union (27)", "Low-income countries", "Upper-middle-income countries", "High-income countries", "Oceania", "Lower-middle-income countries")


covid_deaths_filtered <- 
  covid_deaths %>% 
  filter(!location %in% covid_combined_data) %>%  #filtering out aggregated data
  select(location,
         date,
         stringency_index,
         new_cases,
         new_cases_smoothed,
         new_deaths,
         new_deaths_smoothed,
         new_vaccinations_smoothed,
         population_density) %>% #selecting only variables we are using to clean the data
  mutate(date = ymd(date))  %>% #changed the structure of date from string to date format
  drop_na(new_cases_smoothed, 
          new_deaths_smoothed, 
          new_vaccinations_smoothed) #dropping NA values

#Saving all the excess variables we want to drop to make the code easier to read
drop_columns <- 
  c("RegionName", "RegionCode", "C1M_Flag", "C2M_Flag", "C3M_Flag", "C4M_Flag", "C5M_Flag", "C6M_Flag", "C7M_Flag", "E1_Flag","H1_Flag","H6M_Flag","H7_Flag","H8M_Flag", "M1_Wildcard", "V2B", "V2C", "V2D", "V2E", "V2F", "V2G", "V3G", "V3" )

covid_stringency_filtered <- 
  covid_stringency %>% 
  select(-contains(drop_columns)) %>% #selecting only variables we are using to clean the data
  mutate(date = ymd(Date)) %>% #changed the structure of date from string to date format
  rename_with(~ gsub(" ", "_",.), #variables had spaces in them, replacing with _ to avoid errors
              everything()) %>%
  rename("location" = "CountryName") %>%
  full_join(covid_deaths_filtered, 
            by = c("location", "date")) %>%
  mutate(across(c(
    C1M_School_closing, 
    C2M_Workplace_closing, 
    C3M_Cancel_public_events, 
    C4M_Restrictions_on_gatherings, 
    C5M_Close_public_transport, 
    C6M_Stay_at_home_requirements, 
    H1_Public_information_campaigns, 
    C7M_Restrictions_on_internal_movement, 
    C8EV_International_travel_controls,
    `V4_Mandatory_Vaccination_(summary)`, 
    E1_Income_support), 
  as.factor)) # Factoring these becayse they are  all ordinal variables according to the code book, but were saved as numerical.

Calculating Stringency Levels

We are assigning each country a Stringency Level: High, Medium, Low.

Stringency levels for each country changed over the three years, which is why we average the stringency over the three years to give countries an overall level.

We categorized them using percentiles, countries that fell below the 25th percentile were assigned to Low Stringency, countries between the 25th and 75th percentile were assigned to Medium Stringency and countries above the 75th percentile were assigned to High Stringency.

We calculate the number of countries that fell in each group just to make sure the each group is big enough for the analysis to be valid.

#calculating Avg stringency over the 3 years to categorize countries
avg_stringency_calc <- 
  covid_deaths_filtered %>%
  group_by(location) %>%
  drop_na(stringency_index) %>%
  summarize(avg_stringency = mean(stringency_index, 
                                  rm.na = TRUE))

#finding percentiles for Avg Stringency
low_threshold <- 
  quantile(avg_stringency_calc$avg_stringency, 
                          0.25)
high_threshold <- 
  quantile(avg_stringency_calc$avg_stringency, 
                           0.75)

#using the percentiles to assign countries stringency level
avg_stringency_calc <- 
  avg_stringency_calc %>%
  mutate(stringency_level = case_when(
    avg_stringency >= high_threshold ~ "High Stringency",
    avg_stringency >= low_threshold ~ "Medium Stringency",
    TRUE ~ "Low Stringency")) %>%
  mutate(stringency_level = factor(stringency_level, levels = c("High Stringency", "Medium Stringency", "Low Stringency"))) %>%
  rename("id" = "location")

World Map Graphs

Creating a Map to visualize Stringency level across the world. First some data cleaning to create a consolidated map dataset.

#found long and lat data for countries
world_map <- 
  world_map %>%
  rename(id = region, 
         x = long,
         y = lat) %>%
  mutate(id = case_when(
    id == "USA" ~ "United States",
    id == "UK" ~ "United Kingdom",
    id == "Democratic Republic of the Congo" ~ "Democratic Republic of Congo",
    id == "Republic of Congo" ~ "Congo",
    id == "Ivory Coast" ~ "Cote d'Ivoire",
    id == "Czech Republic" ~ "Czechia", 
    TRUE ~ id
  )) #There were discrepancies in country names between world map data and our data set, so fixed those so all countries with data are properly mapped

#Combining the stringency_levels back into mapping data set.   
world_map <- 
  world_map %>%
  inner_join(avg_stringency_calc, by = "id")

#countries that had NA values were not being mapped, so we created a complete list of all countries, and then joined with the stringency calculation so the data set records countries with NA values. This allowed the map to record those without data in grey rather than being left blank 
countries_list <- 
  world_map %>%
  group_by(id) %>%
  select(id) %>%
  distinct(id)

world_map<- 
  countries_list %>% 
  left_join(world_map, 
            by = "id")

Categorizing High and Low Income Countries

We are aware that the existing data set extracted from Oxford does aggregate High and Low income countries. However, it was unclear how this was categorized, therefore we decided to categorize these countries ourself using World Banks methodology.

Here is how the World Bank has catagorized the countries. * Low-income countries are those with a gross national income (GNI) per capita of $1,145 or less in 2023. * Lower-middle-income countries are those with a GNI per capita between $1,146 and 4,515 in 2023. * Upper-middle-income countries are those with a GNI per capita between $4,516 and 14,005 in 2023. * High-income countries are those with a GNI per capita of more than $14,005 in 2023.

For the preliminary analysis, we used 2020 as the base year in categorizing the countries.

#combing income level data with mapping data

world_map <- 
  income_categories %>%
  rename(id = Entity, income_level = `World Bank's income classification`) %>%
  filter(Year == 2020) %>%
  select(-Year) %>%
  right_join(world_map, by = "id")

Descriptive Graphs

This code creates bar graphs showing how countries are distributed across different categories, such as school closures or workplace restrictions, by income level. The function groups the data, counts the countries in each category, and the loop makes it easy to generate 9 graphs for each category, with appropriate titles and labels.

#joining income data with stringency data 

covid_stringency_filtered <- 
  income_categories %>%
  rename(location = Entity, income_level = `World Bank's income classification`) %>% # Renaming columns for clarity
  filter(Year == 2020) %>%
  select(-Year) %>% #cleaning unwanted variables 
  right_join(covid_stringency_filtered, by = "location")

# Function to plot bar graphs

plot_bar_graph <- function(data,
                           income_var,
                           cat_variable, 
                           country_var,
                           title = "Distribution by Income Level", 
                           x_label = "Category", 
                           y_label = "Number of Countries") {
  
  data_grouped <- 
  data %>%
  filter(!is.na({{income_var}}), 
         !is.na({{cat_variable}})) %>%
  group_by({{income_var}}, 
           {{cat_variable}}) %>%
  summarise(
    country_count = n_distinct({{country_var}}),  # Count distinct countries
    .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate({{income_var}} := factor({{income_var}}, 
                               levels = c("Low-income countries", 
                                          "Lower-middle-income countries", 
                                          "Upper-middle-income countries", 
                                          "High-income countries")),
         {{cat_variable}} := factor({{cat_variable}}))


plot <- 
  data_grouped %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = {{cat_variable}}, y = country_count, fill = {{income_var}})) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") + 
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Blues") +  # Optional: Set a color palette
  labs(
    title = title,
    x = x_label,
    y = y_label,
    fill = "Income Level"
  ) +
  theme_bw()

return(plot)

}                      

# Function to clean variable names for graph titles
clean_variable_name <- function(var_name) {
  # Remove the leading codes (before the first underscore) and replace underscores with spaces
  cleaned_name <- gsub("^[A-Za-z0-9]+_", "", var_name)  # Remove code part at the start
  cleaned_name <- gsub("_", " ", cleaned_name)  # Replace underscores with spaces
  return(cleaned_name)
}


# List of variables to plot
variables <- c(
  "C1M_School_closing", 
  "C2M_Workplace_closing", 
  "C3M_Cancel_public_events", 
  "C4M_Restrictions_on_gatherings", 
  "C5M_Close_public_transport", 
  "C6M_Stay_at_home_requirements", 
  "H1_Public_information_campaigns", 
  "C7M_Restrictions_on_internal_movement", 
  "C8EV_International_travel_controls",
  "V4_Mandatory_Vaccination_(summary)", 
  "E1_Income_support"
)

# Loop to create and print the plots for all variables in the list
for (var in variables) {
  
  clean_title <- clean_variable_name(var)
  
  plot <- plot_bar_graph(
    data = covid_stringency_filtered,
    income_var = income_level,
    country_var = location, 
    cat_variable = !!sym(var),  # Dynamically get the variable name
    title = paste("Distribution of", clean_title, "by Income Level"),
    x_label = clean_title,
    y_label = "Number of Countries"
  )
  
  print(plot)
}

Cases Regression Model

# Step 1: Lag the dependent and independent variables
covid_data_lagged <- covid_stringency_filtered %>%
  mutate(
    lag_covid_deaths = lag(new_deaths_smoothed, 14),
    lag_covid_cases = lag(new_cases_smoothed, 14),  # 14-day lag for dependent variable
    lag_C1M_School_closing = lag(C1M_School_closing, 21),
    lag_C2M_Workplace_closing = lag(C2M_Workplace_closing, 21),
    lag_C3M_Cancel_public_events = lag(C3M_Cancel_public_events, 21),
    lag_C4M_Restrictions_on_gatherings = lag(C4M_Restrictions_on_gatherings, 21),
    lag_C5M_Close_public_transport = lag(C5M_Close_public_transport, 21),
    lag_C6M_Stay_at_home_requirements = lag(C6M_Stay_at_home_requirements, 21),
    lag_H1_Public_information_campaigns = lag(H1_Public_information_campaigns, 21),
    lag_C7M_Restrictions_on_internal_movement = lag(C7M_Restrictions_on_internal_movement, 21),
    lag_C8EV_International_travel_controls = lag(C8EV_International_travel_controls, 21), 
    lag_V4_Mandatory_Vaccination = lag(`V4_Mandatory_Vaccination_(summary)`, 21), 
    lag_covid_vaccines = lag(new_vaccinations_smoothed, 21), 
    lag_healthcare_infrastructure = lag(H4_Emergency_investment_in_healthcare, 21),
    lag_income_support = lag(E1_Income_support, 21)
  )

# Step 2: Remove rows with NA values caused by lagging
covid_data_lagged <- covid_data_lagged %>% drop_na()

# Step 3: Fit the regression model
reg_model_cases <- lm(
  new_cases_smoothed ~ lag_covid_cases +
    lag_C1M_School_closing + 
    lag_C2M_Workplace_closing + 
    lag_C3M_Cancel_public_events +
    lag_C4M_Restrictions_on_gatherings + 
    lag_C5M_Close_public_transport +
    lag_C6M_Stay_at_home_requirements + 
    lag_H1_Public_information_campaigns +
    lag_C7M_Restrictions_on_internal_movement + 
    lag_C8EV_International_travel_controls + 
    lag_covid_vaccines + 
    lag_income_support + 
    lag_healthcare_infrastructure +
    population_density,
  data = covid_data_lagged
)

# Step 4: View the regression summary
summary(reg_model_cases)

    lag_covid_vaccines + lag_income_support + lag_healthcare_infrastructure + 
    population_density, data = covid_data_lagged)

plotting the reg models

The code extracts and visualizes the regression coefficients from two models (reg_model_cases and reg_model_death) along with their 95% confidence intervals using ggplot2. It generates horizontal bar plots to show the estimated effect of each predictor on the outcome variables, with error bars representing the confidence intervals.

# Extract coefficients
coeffs_cases <- tidy(reg_model_cases, conf.int = TRUE) %>%
  filter(term != "(Intercept)")

# Plot coefficients
ggplot(coeffs_cases, aes(x = reorder(term, estimate), y = estimate)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), width = 0.3) +
  coord_flip() +  # Flip for easier reading
  labs(title = "Cases Model: Regression Coefficients", x = "Predictors", y = "Estimate") +
  theme_bw() 
# Extract coefficients
coeffs_death <- tidy(reg_model_death, conf.int = TRUE) %>%
  filter(term != "(Intercept)")

# Plot coefficients
ggplot(coeffs_death, aes(x = reorder(term, estimate), y = estimate)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), width = 0.3) +
  coord_flip() +  # Flip for easier reading
  labs(title = "Death Model: Regression Coefficients", x = "Predictors", y = "Estimate") +
  theme_bw()
